issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette:
Ravi Patel was 41 when he came to treatment, a married South Asian American man who worked as a graphic designer for a mid-sized marketing firm. He described the event he could not seem to put into words as something that happened during a late drive home, when he was pulled over by police after a small car fire on the shoulder had filled part of the road with smoke. What stayed with him most sharply was the smell first: burnt rubber and something electrical in the air, thick enough that he noticed it before he understood why traffic had slowed. There were flashing lights ahead and officers redirecting cars. Ravi remembered one officer motioning him over, then another approaching his window. He had initially felt relieved to see authority present, assuming they would help sort out the confusion. Instead, the interaction turned adversarial. He was ordered out of the car, questioned in a way he experienced as accusatory, and restrained while trying to explain that he had simply been passing through. He has said that someone he had trusted had told him before that cooperating fully would keep him safe, and during the encounter that belief seemed to collapse. When he looks back now, what floods him is not only fear but intense guilt, as if he should have said something differently, stayed calmer, anticipated the officers’ reactions, or prevented what followed.

In the weeks afterward, Ravi found that he could replay the scene in fragments but struggled to narrate it from beginning to end. He would start to tell his wife what happened at the roadside, get as far as the smoke, the uniforms, the commands, and then lose the thread completely. He often said, frustrated, that he knew exactly what had happened but could not find the words. The more he tried to explain clearly, the more his mind seemed to seize up around certain moments. What came through instead were conclusions that felt firm and global: people could not be trusted, the world was dangerous, and betrayal could come from the very people or systems one was supposed to rely on.

Ravi’s days narrowed around these convictions. At work, where he spent long hours in an open-plan office designing logos, packaging, and digital campaigns, he became preoccupied with scanning the room and the hallway beyond it. If a security guard or building employee in uniform crossed the lobby downstairs, Ravi felt his body tense before he had fully registered why. He took longer routes back from lunch to avoid passing the front desk when police officers occasionally entered the building for routine calls in the neighborhood. On one occasion a burnt smell from an overheated office microwave drifted across the studio, and he had to step outside, standing on the sidewalk with his chest tight, trying to steady himself before going back in. He did not tell coworkers much. He had come to believe that if he spoke carelessly, he could be misread again, and so before almost any interaction—meeting a client, answering a question from his supervisor, even returning a phone call—he rehearsed what to say in his head. He tried out sentences, revised them, imagined how they might be interpreted, then revised them again.

At home, his wife noticed how difficult it had become for him to think ahead. Ravi avoided making plans for trips, gatherings, or even small things a few weeks away. When she asked about visiting family or booking time off, he would say they should wait and see. He did not describe this as indecision so much as a refusal to lean into a future that no longer felt dependable. He moved through public spaces watchfully, vigilant for dangerous people, paying close attention to faces, posture, who was watching whom, who might suddenly exercise power. What frightened him most was not only that harm could happen, but that it could happen in full view of authority, or through authority, while he was left trying and failing to explain himself.

By the time Ravi sought help, the strain had become visible in both his marriage and his work. His wife was upset by how often he pulled away from conversations about what had happened and by how little he would commit to anything beyond the next few days. At work he was still performing, but deadlines felt harder because ordinary communication took so much preparation. He came in describing exhaustion, shame, and a deep sense that he was no longer living as the person he had been before that night. What finally brought him to treatment was a recent incident in the office lobby, when two uniformed officers walked in as he was leaving and the faint smell of something burnt from a food cart outside hit him at the same moment. He froze, then went back upstairs and sat at his desk unable to speak. He said he was afraid that if he did not get help, his life would go on shrinking around these moments; what he hoped for, though he said it cautiously, was to be able to tell the story straight through and not feel taken over by it every time the world reminded him.
